description: Two people interested in making a change through machine learning
summary: Dipole is a free website that shows how fast every part of the planet warmed compared with the world as a whole, using NASA’s GISTEMP temperature record from 1900 to 2025. A single global average hides opposite stories. Since 1980 the Arctic has warmed 3.3 times faster than the world, while since 1900 the ocean south of Greenland has barely warmed at all. Visitors can play through the years, select any place or city, see how many people live where warming outpaced the world, and compare how much water northwest India held after each monsoon using NASA’s GRACE satellites. Every number comes with its uncertainty and a plain-language explanation.
details:
Climate change is usually reported as one global number. Dipole shows what that number hides. It is a free website where anyone can pick a place on Earth and see how fast it warmed compared with the world, using NASA's GISTEMP temperature record from 1900 to 2025. Select a grid square, a city or your own location, and a panel explains in plain language what changed, by how much and how sure we are. You can also press Play to watch the years go by, or follow a guided tour. Three findings stood out. The ocean south of Greenland has barely warmed since 1900 (+0.01 °C per decade, against +0.10 for the world). Since 1980 the Arctic has warmed 3.3 times faster than the world. Over 1921–2025 that lead shrinks to about 1.6 times, so most of the Arctic's extra warming is recent. We also link temperature to people and water: 38.8% of Indians live in places that warmed faster than the world since 1900, and NASA's GRACE satellites show northwest India holding about 31 cm less water after the monsoon in 2018–2025 than in 2004–2009.

The creative part is the question itself: comparing every place with the planet, which brings out opposite stories side by side. We built the analysis in Python (NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, netCDF4, Rasterio) and the site in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript on GitHub Pages, with no server or login, so it works on any phone.

We hope Dipole helps students, teachers, and journalists see what the global numbers hide, what happens where they live, and how confident we can be about it.
